support.quote:
The GRC testing was conducted using the centrifuge test facility in the ZGRF 5.2 second drop tower (Fig. 6).3 The 
chamber is 299 l in volume with an I.D.
of 81.2 cm and an internal height if 30.5 cm.

To achieve lunar gravity, the 
chamber was rotated at 20.4 RPM for several minutes before the drop (I.e.

onset of microgravity) to bring the air in 
the chamber to near solid body rotation.

In this configuration, (during the drop) the gravity vector was radially 
outwards, and the resulting buoyant flow was radially inward To achieve upward spread the long axis of the sample 
is oriented radially and ignited on the outside edge so the resulting buoyant flow is concurrent with the direction of 
flame spread.
Owing to the short radius of rotation, there was a significant gravity gradient.

The flames, however, 
(especially when near the extinction limits) did not spread significantly during the drop, so the g-variation was 
considered to have a minimal impact on the results.

The short radius of rotation also caused a significant Coriolis force 
in the tangential direction19.

Initial tests found that the effect was mitigated by orienting the sample surface parallel to 
the axis of rotation (long edge down) so the Coriolis flow was impeded by the sample surface.

The igniter was a 
ceramic igniter very similar to the one used at WSTF except it withdrew vertically.

To increase the number of tests 
for repeatability, two samples were ignited and tested in each drop.

The samples were several cm apart and offset 
vertically (Fig. 6) so they did not interfere with each other.

The ignition region of the sample was exposed to a slow 
flow (~30 cm/s) of gas with an oxygen concentration 5 to 10% higher than the ambient.

This enabled sample ignition 
in a chamber condition where the sample might be near the flammability limit.

During the ignition interval, the drop 
rig is hanging at the top of the tower and is spinning to produce a 1/6 g radial acceleration in addition to the 1-g vertical 
force.

This resulting buoyant flow primarily directed laterally across the sample is less successful at heating the 
unburned sample than the purely upward flow at WSTF.

The drop tower operations require the system to operate 
autonomously so the entire process was controlled automatically by the drop rig.

The ignition duration and the oxygen 
enhancement were varied based on experience with ignitability of the material being tested.

After a prescribed 
duration, the igniter is turned off and retracted.

One second later, the oxygen enhanced flow is turned off and the 
package is released.
At this point, the flow is entirely driven by buoyancy.

Since the bulk of the chamber is already at 
the target atmosphere, the buoyant flow immediately sweeps in the target conditions.

Both samples were observed 
with separate front and edge view cameras.
